blocks.text: “Good Heaven, my dear little woman,” he said, “how did you get here? Who would have expected to see you! Is anything wrong? Is Ada well?”
“Ah!” he said, leaning back in his chair. “My poor cousin! I was writing to you, Esther.”

He looked so tired and worn out, with such a thin, worried face! And yet he was still young and handsome, in the full strength of his youth. He leaned back in his chair and crushed the closely written sheet of paper in his hand.
“Have you taken the trouble to write all that, and now I am not going to read it after all?” I asked.
“Oh my dear,” he answered, with a hopeless movement of his hand. “You can read it in the whole room. It is all over here.”
I gently begged him not to lose hope. I told him that I had heard by chance that he was in difficulty. I had come to talk with him about what could best be done.

“That is like you, Esther. But it is useless, and so it is not like you!” he said with a sad smile. “I am going away on leave today. I would have left in another hour. The leave is there to make things go quietly while I sell my position as an officer. Well! Let the past stay in the past. So this career goes the same way as all the others. I only need to have been in the Church too. Then I would have tried every one of the professions.”
“Richard,” I said, pressing him, “it is not as hopeless as that?”

“Esther,” he answered, “it really is. I am so close to disgrace that the people in authority over me (as the catechism says) would much rather be without me than have me. And they are right. I have debts, and people keep demanding that I pay them. There are other problems like that too. But even apart from all that, I am not fit even for this job. I have no care, no mind, no heart, no soul for anything except one thing. Why, if this bubble had not burst now,” he said, as he tore the letter he had written into small pieces. He threw them away gloomily, a few at a time. “How could I have gone abroad? I would surely have been ordered abroad. But how could I have gone? I know that thing too well. How could I trust even Vholes, unless I was right there behind him!”
I suppose he could tell from my face what I was going to say. But he took the hand I had put on his arm. He touched my lips with it to stop me from going on.

“No, Dame Durden! There are two subjects I forbid. I must forbid them. The first is John Jarndyce. The second, you know what it is. Call it madness, if you like. I tell you I can't help it now, and I can't be sane. But it is not madness at all. It is the one goal I have to follow. It is a pity that anyone ever persuaded me to leave my road for any other. It would be wise to give it up now, after all the time, worry and effort I have put into it! Oh yes, truly wise. It would please some people very much, too. But I never will.”

He was in such a mood that I thought it best not to argue against him. That might only make him more determined, if anything could make him more determined. I took out Ada's letter and put it in his hand.
“Am I to read it now?” he asked.

When I told him yes, he put it on the table. He rested his head on his hand and began to read. He had not read far when he rested his head on both hands. He did this to hide his face from me. After a little while he got up, as if the light were bad, and went to the window. He finished reading it there, with his back to me. After he had finished and folded it up, he stood there for some minutes with the letter in his hand. When he came back to his chair, I saw tears in his eyes.
“Of course, Esther, you know what she says here?” He spoke in a softer voice, and he kissed the letter as he asked me.

“She offers me,” he went on, tapping his foot on the floor, “the little money that she is sure to inherit so soon. It is just as little and as much as I have wasted. And she begs and prays me to take it. She wants me to use it to put my affairs right, and to stay in the army.”
